---
title: "Variance and covariance"
execute:
  enabled: true
  echo: true
  warning: false
  message: false
---

The [expected value page](expected-values.qmd) summarized the center of a distribution. But the mean does not say how tightly probability is concentrated around that center. We now measure spread in the [CMUdict total phone-count distribution](why-random-variables.qmd#the-pronunciation-entry-outcomes) and then ask how vowel and consonant counts vary together.

We derive variance from squared centered distances, explain why the squaring is needed, and then extend the same centered-product logic to covariance and a variance decomposition.

```{r}
#| label: load-cmudict-variance
library(ggplot2)

cmu <- read.csv(
  "data/cmudict/cmudict-pronunciations.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  check.names = FALSE,
  na.strings = ""
)
cmu$consonant_phone_count <- cmu$phone_count - cmu$vowel_phone_count

phone_pmf <- as.data.frame(table(cmu$phone_count))
names(phone_pmf) <- c("phone_count", "entries")
phone_pmf$phone_count <- as.integer(as.character(phone_pmf$phone_count))
phone_pmf$mass <- phone_pmf$entries / nrow(cmu)

mean_phone_count <- sum(phone_pmf$phone_count * phone_pmf$mass)
phone_pmf$deviation <- phone_pmf$phone_count - mean_phone_count
phone_pmf$variance_contribution <- phone_pmf$deviation^2 * phone_pmf$mass
phone_variance <- sum(phone_pmf$variance_contribution)
signed_deviation_mean <- sum(phone_pmf$deviation * phone_pmf$mass)

mean_vowels <- mean(cmu$vowel_phone_count)
mean_consonants <- mean(cmu$consonant_phone_count)
vowel_variance <- mean((cmu$vowel_phone_count - mean_vowels)^2)
consonant_variance <- mean((cmu$consonant_phone_count - mean_consonants)^2)
vowel_consonant_covariance <- mean(
  (cmu$vowel_phone_count - mean_vowels) *
    (cmu$consonant_phone_count - mean_consonants)
)
decomposed_variance <-
  vowel_variance + consonant_variance + 2 * vowel_consonant_covariance

stopifnot(
  nrow(cmu) == 133854L,
  abs(signed_deviation_mean) < 1e-12,
  abs(phone_variance -
        mean((cmu$phone_count - mean(cmu$phone_count))^2)) < 1e-12,
  abs(phone_variance - decomposed_variance) < 1e-10
)

c(phone_variance = phone_variance,
  vowel_variance = vowel_variance,
  consonant_variance = consonant_variance,
  vowel_consonant_covariance = vowel_consonant_covariance,
  decomposed_phone_variance = decomposed_variance)
```

## Variance as expected squared distance

We need to average distance from the mean without letting positive and negative deviations cancel. The [**variance**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html) does this by summarizing expected squared distance:

$$
\operatorname{Var}[X]
\equiv
\mathbb{E}\!\left[(X-\mathbb{E}[X])^2\right].
$$

For the empirical PMF,

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(X)
=\sum_x (x-\widehat{\mathbb{E}}[X])^2\widehat p_X(x).
$$

The result is `r sprintf("%.3f", phone_variance)` phones squared. This is the population variance of the finite empirical distribution, so the displayed code divides by the number of entries rather than using the sample-variance denominator.

For a three-value hand calculation, give $1$, $2$, and $4$ equal mass. Their
mean is $7/3$, and <!-- dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation -->

$$
\operatorname{Var}[X]
=\frac{1}{3}\left[ % dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation
\left(1-\frac73\right)^2+
\left(2-\frac73\right)^2+
\left(4-\frac73\right)^2
\right]
=\frac{14}{9}. % dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation
$$
<!-- dqr-allow: symbolic-derivation -->

The CMUdict code performs the same sequence: compute the mean, subtract it from
each value, square, weight by empirical mass, and sum.

```{r}
#| label: plot-cmudict-variance-contributions
#| fig-cap: "Contribution of each observed phone count to the empirical population variance."
ggplot(phone_pmf, aes(phone_count, variance_contribution)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey65", width = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "Phones in pronunciation",
       y = "Contribution to variance (phones squared)") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The rare, long pronunciations contribute more than their small masses alone would suggest because variance squares their distances from the mean.

## Why square the deviations?

The expected signed deviation is

$$
\mathbb{E}[X-\mathbb{E}[X]]=0.
$$

The code verifies this identity up to floating-point precision. Squaring prevents cancellation and gives greater weight to larger departures. Variance is thus sensitive to probability placed far from the mean.

## Covariance and a variance decomposition

The [**covariance**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html) of vowel count $V$ and consonant count $C$ is

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(V,C)
\equiv
\mathbb{E}\!\left[(V-\mathbb{E}[V])(C-\mathbb{E}[C])\right].
$$

The empirical covariance is `r sprintf("%.3f", vowel_consonant_covariance)` phones squared. Positive covariance means that entries with more vowel phones tend also to contain more consonant phones, relative to their respective means. It does not by itself identify a phonological mechanism.

Because $X=V+C$,

$$
\operatorname{Var}[X]
=\operatorname{Var}[V]
+\operatorname{Var}[C]
+2\operatorname{Cov}(V,C).
$$

The displayed assertion checks this decomposition directly from the pronunciation entries.

Covariance appears here because it is the cross-term created when
$(V+C-\mathbb{E}[V+C])^2$ is expanded. The later
[covariance page](covariance.qmd) treats covariance as the focal summary of a
joint distribution and distinguishes empirical-population and sample-estimator
conventions.

## Keeping the units visible

If phone count is measured in phones, each deviation is measured in phones. Squaring produces phones squared. Squared units make variance useful for algebra but less direct as a descriptive distance. [Standard deviation](standard-deviation.qmd) takes a square root to return to the original units.

Variance also requires the expected squared deviation to be finite. A variable can have a finite mean but place enough probability far from that mean for its variance to be infinite.

## Check your understanding

1. Recompute the population variance of `vowel_phone_count` from its empirical PMF and compare it with `vowel_variance`.
2. Why is the expected signed deviation zero even though the variance is positive?
3. Which term would vanish from the variance decomposition if vowel and consonant counts had zero covariance?
4. Why does the empirical covariance not imply that adding vowels causes consonants to be added?
5. A student computes the average signed deviation and reports zero variance.
   Which step in the definition was omitted?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The empirical PMF gives $\operatorname{Var}[V]=0.975784$ vowel phones squared, matching `vowel_variance`. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. Signed deviations above and below the mean cancel to zero, while squaring prevents that cancellation and yields positive variance. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. If vowel and consonant counts had zero covariance, the term $2\operatorname{Cov}[V,C]$ would vanish from $\operatorname{Var}[V+C]$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. The covariance describes co-variation among pronunciation entries; it does not identify an intervention in which adding vowels causes consonants to be added. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
5. The deviations must be squared before they are averaged. Unsquared positive
   and negative deviations cancel by construction.

</details>

Variance is an expected squared distance, with squaring preventing positive and
negative deviations from canceling. Covariance appears as the cross-term in
the variance of a sum. The [next page](standard-deviation.qmd) returns the
spread measure to the original units.
